episode_title: Flexible circadian detection, biobank-scale synthetic genomes, and peering inside ESMFold's folding trunk

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Morning. It's October twenty-eighth, and the archive and the bio-archive put out around thirty-four new preprints overnight.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Decent haul. Today we've got a new way to find circadian rhythms in messy transcriptomic time courses, someone cracking open ESMFold's trunk with sparse autoencoders to see what it's actually computing, and a flow-matching model generating synthetic whole genomes from the UK Biobank.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Plus a growth-coupled strain design ranker and an out-of-distribution detector for clinical methylation classifiers. Let's start with the circadian one.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: This is CircaFMM, paper one in the show notes. The problem is familiar to anyone who's tried to call rhythmic genes from human or field-collected transcriptomic data: the classic cosinor test fits a fixed sinusoid, but real sampling is irregular and a lot of genuine circadian expression profiles are asymmetric, not clean sine waves.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So what's the actual trick, beyond just saying cosinor is too rigid?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: They build on something called the Frequency Modulated Möbius model, FMM, which was already used in other time-series contexts. The key move is defining rhythmicity through a single phase parameter that can warp the waveform shape, so the non-rhythmic null is just a flat, time-invariant mean rather than a fixed harmonic shape. Around that they add time-density weighting to handle uneven sampling, regularized estimation, and bootstrap calibration of a weighted likelihood-ratio-type statistic, since the test isn't a standard regular one.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And the obvious worry with a more flexible model is overfitting or inflated false positives, especially with few time points per gene.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Which is presumably why the bootstrap calibration is there. In simulations they report controlled type-one error under irregular sampling and better power than the cosinor F-test specifically for asymmetric waveforms. The real test is GTEx's thirteen-tissue postmortem dataset, where time of death sampling is about as irregular as it gets.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Did it just rediscover the usual suspects?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: It recovers the canonical clock genes and circadian pathways, so it's not throwing away the known biology. But it also flags additional rhythmic candidates that have lower signal-to-noise ratio and distinctly non-sinusoidal, asymmetric temporal profiles, genes a cosinor-based scan would likely miss. For anyone doing differential rhythmicity analysis on human postmortem or biobank-style transcriptomic data, where you don't get to control sampling times, this is a genuinely useful addition to the toolkit, and there's a Shiny app and GitHub repo if you want to try it on your own data.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Next up is a very different kind of black-box problem. Paper two looks inside ESMFold, the structure predictor that folds proteins directly from sequence using a neural network trunk instead of multiple sequence alignments. It works remarkably well, but nobody really knows what computation inside the trunk is doing the folding.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Sparse autoencoders have already been used on protein language models like E-S-M-two to pull out interpretable concepts from the dense representations. What's new here?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Those earlier efforts were on sequence models. This is the first time anyone's applied sparse dictionaries to a folding model's trunk, where the job isn't predicting masked amino acids but regressing an actual three-D structure. They do this in three steps. First, they profile how representations are distributed across the trunk's modules and across recycles, ESMFold runs its structure module several times, recycling its own output, to find where distinct spatial computation happens. Second, they train sparse dictionaries separately on the single representation and the pair representation, the pair representation being the per-residue-pair features that essentially encode a distance and contact map. They find a division of labor: the single representation carries over sequence-level semantics inherited from the language model, while the pair representation is where the actual pairwise geometry gets computed.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And the third step?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: They interpret the learned dictionary at scale using a reasoning language model to label the concepts, trace how those concepts combine across blocks with gradient-based attribution, and check whether the traced computation lines up with known biochemistry or departs from it. The headline result is that the sparse features capturing this relational geometry can actually forecast the model's own fold quality, so the concept activations carry a usable signal about when the structure prediction is likely to be good or bad.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: That's the part I'd flag as useful beyond pure mechanistic curiosity. If a concept-based read-out can flag low-confidence folds, that's a cheap, interpretable complement to the usual pLDDT-style confidence scores people already lean on downstream.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Right, and it turns what's normally treated as an opaque regression into something closer to an inspectable circuit, which matters if you're using these structures for anything mechanistic, like modeling protein-DNA or protein-protein interfaces.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper three, HELICS, tackles a genomics problem that's been nagging at population genetics for a while: generating realistic synthetic genotype data at biobank scale. The motivation is data-limited settings, underrepresented ancestries, rare disease cohorts, restricted-access biobanks, where you'd like privacy-preserving synthetic cohorts for benchmarking or augmentation, but the distribution you're trying to learn is genuinely enormous, hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of correlated SNPs.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Haplotype-based genotype simulators already exist. What does this add?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: The headline feature is that it's phasing-free, it skips the haplotype phasing step that existing simulators depend on, which is itself an error-prone preprocessing stage. Mechanically, they tokenize each chromosome with a convolutional autoencoder, compressing more than six hundred thousand SNPs down to four thousand ninety six continuous latent tokens, then train a transformer-based conditional flow matching model over the concatenated multi-chromosome latent space.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Flow matching for the non-ML-native listener is basically the same family as diffusion models, you learn a velocity field that transports noise to data along a chosen interpolation path, and it's become popular because sampling can be more direct than classic diffusion.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Exactly. They train this on over four hundred seventeen thousand UK Biobank genomes. The result is genome-wide synthetic cohorts with stronger fidelity than existing haplotype-based simulators, meaning better allele-frequency agreement in external evaluation and better preservation of both local and long-range SNP correlation structure, which is basically linkage disequilibrium at scale. Conditioning on ancestry and on genetic liability summaries lets them generate cohorts targeted at specific risk profiles, and in a perturbation test, turning up the conditioned disease liability shifts SNP-level dosages in the generated genomes in a way that's highly correlated with published GWAS association weights.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So the latent space has actually learned something that respects known genetic architecture, not just marginal allele frequencies. The catch I'd want addressed is whether the synthetic ancestry diversity is really adding information beyond what's already in UK Biobank's own, fairly skewed, ancestry composition, since a generative model is still bounded by what it was trained on.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Fair, that's not something the abstract can answer, but as a scalable generative framework for SNP-level data it's a notable addition to the genomics toolkit, especially for anyone thinking about privacy-aware data sharing or augmenting rare-disease cohorts.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Paper four moves into metabolic engineering. Growth-coupled strain design means finding gene deletions that force a cell's growth to depend on producing your target compound, so natural selection during fermentation keeps the strain productive instead of drifting away from it. Constraint-based methods, basically flux balance analysis wrapped in a bilevel search, can find these deletion strategies, but you typically have to redo the combinatorial search from scratch for every new target metabolite.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: So what's the actual contribution, beyond another metabolic model wrapper?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: It's a learned ranking step that sits in front of the expensive constraint-based search, so you don't have to brute-force the combinatorics every time. The model, HGPRGDel, explicitly encodes gene-protein-reaction logic, the Boolean structure of which genes jointly support a reaction because they're subunits of the same complex, versus which genes are redundant alternatives like isozymes. That's richer than treating genes and reactions as a simple bipartite graph. It learns from previously curated deletion strategies and produces a continuous priority ranking for candidate genes per target metabolite, which then feeds into adjustable-budget candidate construction and standard constraint-based evaluation.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And across the three genome-scale models they tested, the core E. coli model, the yeast model iMM904, and the larger E. coli model iML1515, it got the best macro F1 and A-U-C among the learning configurations they compared, and recovered on average ninety percent of the reference deletion genes from the MetNetComp database while examining fewer candidate genes than the baselines.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: It's a more applied paper than most of what we cover, strain design rather than gene regulation, but the underlying idea, embedding the actual hypergraph-like logic of a biological network into a learned prioritization model instead of flattening it, is the same philosophy you see in gene regulatory network inference. Worth knowing even if you're not doing bioproduction.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Last deep dive, paper five, is about keeping clinical methylation classifiers honest. DNA methylation array classifiers are used clinically to type tumors, brain tumor classification is probably the best known example, but a model trained on a fixed reference cohort has no way to know when it's looking at a tumor type it's never seen, it'll just confidently assign the closest label it has.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So this is out-of-distribution detection bolted onto that pipeline. What's actually new about their setup?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: They train deep classifiers on two public cohorts, a sarcoma cohort and a brain tumor cohort, pull embeddings from the bottleneck layer at two sizes, two hundred and five hundred dimensions, and then systematically compare five different out-of-distribution scoring methods on those embeddings: one-dimensional subspace analysis, k-nearest neighbors, ridge regression, Mahalanobis distance, and sum of squared distances. They use something called spectral discrepancy to separate in-distribution from out-of-distribution samples, which essentially measures how much a new sample's feature structure deviates from the low-rank subspace the embedding has learned to represent.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And which method won, and does it actually generalize?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: One-dimensional subspace analysis was the most effective across the board. Treating sarcoma as the known distribution and brain tumors as out-of-distribution, they got an A-U-C of zero point nine seven five; the reverse direction gave zero point nine five seven. The part that matters most clinically is the independent test set, not just cross-validation, where they still got a mean A-U-C of zero point nine seven six and a true negative rate at ninety five percent sensitivity of zero point nine three five.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: That independent clinical validation is the detail I'd have pushed on if it were missing, so it's good it's there. As a quality-control layer sitting in front of any sequencing-or-array-based tumor classifier, this kind of out-of-distribution check seems like something that should just become standard practice before these models go near a diagnostic report.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Let's move faster through the rest. Paper six takes a genuine physics approach to neuronal growth, deriving a stochastic path action from Langevin and Fokker-Planck models of axons growing on periodic micropatterned substrates, where the most probable growth trajectory is literally a minimum-action path. For substrates with varying stiffness, they derive a separate Fermat-like spatial action with an effective refractive index set by traction and stiffness, predicting axon turning at stiffness boundaries with an approximate Snell's law and a critical angle. It's a nice reminder that variational principles aren't just for physics undergrads, they connect measurable quantities like drift, diffusion and traction to the global shape of a growing axon, useful if you're designing biomimetic substrates for regeneration.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Paper seven is a software note, scPyviewer, a Python-native interactive viewer for AnnData objects, aimed at labs tired of converting scanpy output into Seurat just to get a shareable viewer. Against three established R Shiny tools it matches or beats feature parity, and on large datasets, up to around three hundred thirteen thousand cells, it renders faster and uses far less memory, with Seurat-based tools reportedly running out of an eight gigabyte limit entirely. It also exposes a Python API returning Matplotlib figures and pandas tables, so it slots directly into a scanpy workflow instead of sitting beside it.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper eight is pyTransRate, a modern Python reimplementation of TransRate, the reference-free scoring tool for de novo transcriptome assemblies that most people stopped being able to install because it needed an ancient Ruby version. The new version runs on current snap-aligner and salmon releases, reproduces the original's sequence metrics and read counts exactly, and ranks assemblies consistently with the original across over five thousand paired comparisons, even though the read-based scores themselves aren't numerically identical. Mostly a reproducibility fix, but a useful one if you're still assembling non-model organism transcriptomes without a reference.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Paper nine is a bit of a left-field entry, ACOR, a streaming consensus reconstruction method for DNA storage, where digital information gets encoded into synthetic DNA strands and recovered by sequencing. Instead of waiting for a full read cluster before reconstructing a strand, it keeps a persistent ledger of k-mer transitions and boundary support as reads arrive, then decodes with a length-constrained beam search. On their own wet-lab sequencing library it handled over ten million reads with near-complete recovery in roughly a second, and the parallel version is reported to be tens to over a thousand times faster than their serial baselines, so it's aimed at real-time readout during sequencing rather than after.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper ten steps outside biology for a moment, a large study of over five million webpages tracking how much of the public web contains AI-generated text, using a Bayesian hierarchical model to correct for detector false positive and false negative rates. The AI-generated share has risen sharply but unevenly, higher in English and on dot-com domains than dot-gov or dot-edu, and growing fastest on the least central, least connected pages on the web. Not biology, but the detector-calibration approach is a reasonable template if you ever need to correct for a noisy classifier's error rates when estimating a prevalence.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Paper eleven is a machine learning systems paper on compressing the recurrent state in Mamba-2 language models. They find the state's energy is concentrated in a near rank-one direction that the model barely reads from, while the information the output actually uses lives in a separate low-dimensional subspace not aligned with the raw coordinates. Their method targets that write-read subspace directly with a balanced truncation transform, plus a layer-wise rank allocation scheme, halving state size with noticeably less perplexity loss than a prior baseline. Mostly relevant if you're running long-context genomic sequence models built on state-space architectures rather than transformers.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper twelve is a genuinely fun aside, a Bayesian mixture-of-experts model for the Ballon d'Or's ranked ballots, treating different journalists as belonging to different latent voting styles and using region and similarity terms to separate geography from personal affinity. Applied to the real ballots, removing voting-style similarity effects would have pushed Messi's win probability in twenty-nineteen up from zero point four nine to zero point seven six under a hypothetical new jury from the same countries. Nothing to do with biology, just a nicely built partial-ranking model.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Paper thirteen is squarely biostatistics: relaxed Multisource Exchangeability Models, or MEMs, which borrow historical trial data to boost power in small samples, useful for rare disease trials. The relaxed versions loosen the usual limits on how much borrowing is allowed, and in simulations and a cystic fibrosis trial example they get noticeably more borrowing with only a small increase in bias and generally lower variance than standard MEMs.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper fourteen addresses a very different kind of trust problem, auditing whether a relay or reseller API is actually serving the large language model you paid for. Their method, distributional fingerprint auditing, repeatedly asks simple finite-choice questions, compares response distributions against a trusted reference using a Cauchy combination test, and gets a proper p-value for the audit decision, with good detection across two hundred forty tested model substitution pairs.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And paper fifteen is a digital health reinforcement learning design paper, building an RL system for a forthcoming physical activity trial that personalizes twice-daily activity suggestions. They use an expert-specified causal directed acyclic graph to structure the state representation, handle partially observed rewards, and distribute delayed credit, and calibrate a longitudinal simulator from a previous micro-randomized trial to stress-test the design before real deployment. A good illustration of using causal structure as an engineering tool for RL, even outside the sequencing world.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And rounding out the day, a quick list: a numerical-stability analysis for implicit solvers of stochastic epidemic models, a Bayesian ordinal model for cereal growth-stage scoring in Western Australian oat trials, a finite-population inference method for cross-fitted treatment effect estimators in stratified multistage surveys, a sensitivity analysis for spillover and mediation effects in a cluster-randomized chronic pain trial, an elastic net approach to cause-specific hazard regression using the SANAD epilepsy trial data, an estimate of how a low-nicotine product standard would affect US smoking behavior, a Bayesian model of recovery trajectories after forced sexual experience, practical guidelines for goodness-of-fit testing with right-censored data, a look at what drives battery-swapping preference among UK electric vehicle owners, and a method for reconstructing individual-level Human Development Index scores from survey microdata.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: That's the stack for today. A flexible circadian test for GTEx-style irregular sampling, a first look inside ESMFold's actual folding computation, and a phasing-free way to generate biobank-scale synthetic genomes, with an out-of-distribution safety net for clinical methylation classifiers alongside.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: That's it for this morning. See you tomorrow.

picks.title: CircaFMM: A Flexible Statistical Framework for Circadian Rhythmicity Detection in Transcriptomics
picks.abstract: Detecting circadian rhythmicity in large-scale transcriptomic data is challenging when sampling is irregular, signals are weak, and expression profiles deviate from sinusoidal shapes. The fixed harmonic form of classical Cosinor-based methods may therefore be poorly suited to asymmetric and temporally complex rhythms. We present CircaFMM, a flexible framework for circadian rhythmicity detection based on the single-component Frequency Modulated Möbius (FMM) model. CircaFMM defines rhythmicity as time dependence induced by the Möbius phase parameter, so that the non-rhythmic null corresponds to a time-invariant mean profile. The resulting non-regular test combines time-density weighting, regularized estimation, and bootstrap calibration of a weighted likelihood-ratio-type statistic. Simulations showed controlled type-I error under irregular sampling and improved power over the classical Cosinor F-test for asymmetric waveforms. Applied to the GTEx-13T postmortem transcriptomic dataset, CircaFMM recovered canonical clock genes and circadian pathways while identifying additional rhythmic candidates with lower signal-to-noise-ratio, greater waveform asymmetry, and non-sinusoidal temporal profiles. CircaFMM is available at https://circafmm.shinyapps.io/circafmmshinyapp/, with source code at https://github.com/FMMGroupVa/CircaFMM.
picks.why: A flexible FMM-based alternative to Cosinor models for detecting circadian rhythmicity in irregular, asymmetric transcriptomic time series directly advances the statistical toolkit for sequencing-based gene expression analysis.

picks.title: Structure, Not Sequence: Tracking and Validating Folding Mechanisms in ESMFold's Trunk with Sparse Autoencoders
picks.abstract: Structure predictors like ESMFold fold proteins using neural network computation and have transformed structural biology. However, the driving mechanism from amino-acid (AA) sequence to 3D structure is insufficiently understood, and biological meaning remains locked in the dense network. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promising results in obtaining interpretable concept features over an overcomplete basis of intermediate protein sequence-model representations. Yet folding models, which predict physical shape from AA sequence semantics, have no such account. We hypothesize that the features carrying the folding computation evolve in the 3D structural regression process. In this paper, we interpret the folding trunk in three steps. First, a pilot analysis on the representation distribution across modules and recycles locates distinct spatial computation in the trunk. Second, the dictionaries expose a division of labor: the single representation carries inherited semantics, and the pair representation computes the pairwise geometry. Third, we interpret the dictionary at scale with a reasoning language model, trace how the concepts compose across blocks by gradient-based attribution, and follow the interpreted code to the model's folding output, verifying where the computation aligns with, or departs from, known biochemistry. Together, the sparse dictionaries we train capture the relational geometry the trunk computes beyond the sequence model, and their concept activations forecast the model's own fold quality, turning the black-box folding trunk into a sparse, interpretable, and scientifically verifiable circuit.
picks.why: Using sparse autoencoders to reverse-engineer how ESMFold's trunk computes 3D structure from sequence offers a genuinely novel mechanistic window into structure prediction models that is highly relevant to systems/structural biology methods.

picks.title: HELICS: Biobank-scale Conditional Synthetic Genome Generation via Latent Flow Matching
picks.abstract: Individual-level genotype data underpin genetic discovery, disease-risk modeling, and therapeutic development, yet many critical settings remain data-limited, including underrepresented ancestries, rare or imbalanced disease cohorts, and restricted-access biobanks. Conditional synthetic genome generation would support privacy-aware benchmarking, simulation, and data augmentation, but requires learning an ultra-high-dimensional discrete distribution over hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of correlated single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), or sites of DNA variation. We introduce HELICS: High-fidelity gEneration via Latent Interpolant Conditional Synthesis, a phasing-free latent flow matching framework for genome-wide SNP-level generation from biobank-scale genotype data. HELICS tokenizes chromosomes with convolutional autoencoders, reducing >600K SNPs to 4,096 continuous latent tokens, and trains a transformer parameterized conditional flow matching model over the concatenated multi-chromosome latent representation. Trained on over 417K genomes in the UK Biobank, HELICS generates genome-wide common-variant synthetic cohorts without haplotype phasing and achieves stronger fidelity to real genotypes than existing haplotype-based simulators, including high allele-frequency agreement in external evaluation and superior preservation of local and long-range SNP correlation structure. Conditioning on ancestry and genetic liability summaries enables targeted generation across genetic risk profiles; in perturbation analyses, by increasing the conditioned disease trait liability, HELICS induces SNP-level dosage changes in generated genomes that are highly correlated with published association weights. HELICS provides a scalable generative modeling framework for SNP-level genome data and a path toward conditional synthetic cohorts for data-limited genetic studies.
picks.why: A latent flow-matching generative model for biobank-scale SNP-level synthetic genomes, conditioned on ancestry and disease liability, is a significant methodological advance for genomics data augmentation and privacy-aware cohort simulation.

picks.title: HGPRGDel: GPR-Aware Learning and Ranking for Growth-Coupled Gene Deletion Design
picks.abstract: Designing microbial strains for growth-coupled production, in which cellular growth is linked to the synthesis of a target compound through genetic interventions, is a fundamental goal in metabolic engineering. Constraint-based methods can identify growth-coupled deletion strategies, but design for each target typically requires a separate search across a large number of possible gene-deletion combinations. This motivates a reusable approach that learns from previously evaluated strain designs to prioritize candidate interventions before downstream constraint-based evaluation. We present a reproducible protocol for growth-coupled gene deletion design that learns and ranks gene-deletion priorities for each target metabolite. Using computationally curated deletion strategies as learning resources, the protocol generates continuous deletion-priority rankings, constructs candidate strategies at adjustable search-space budgets, and evaluates these candidates through constraint-based metabolic analysis. Its learning component, HGPRGDel, explicitly represents gene-protein-reaction (GPR) logic, capturing how multiple genes can jointly support a reaction or alternative genes can maintain its activity, while integrating molecular and reaction-level information. Across ecolicore, iMM904, and iML1515, the protocol achieves the highest macro-F1 and AUC among the evaluated learning configurations. HGPRGDel's rankings recovered an average of 90% of the reference deletion genes from MetNetComp by examining fewer genes than the evaluated baseline methods. By separating learned intervention prioritization from downstream constraint-based assessment, the protocol provides a reproducible framework for reusing strain-design knowledge while controlling the size of the candidate space and retaining mechanistic evaluation of growth-coupled production.
picks.why: A GPR-aware learning-to-rank framework for growth-coupled gene deletion design bridges machine learning with constraint-based metabolic modeling, directly relevant to systems biology and strain engineering.

picks.title: Enhancing Clinical Classifier Robustness with Deep Representation Learning Based OOD Detection on DNA Methylation Data
picks.abstract: DNA methylation (DNAM) array-based tumor classification is a powerful clinical diagnostic tool, but models trained on fixed reference cohorts can produce faulty predictions for tumor types not represented in the training distribution. We propose an end-to-end deep representation learning-based out-of-distribution (OOD) detection framework for DNAm array data. Deep neural network (DNN) classifiers were trained on public sarcoma (SARC) (GSE140686) and brain tumor (BT) (GSE90496) cohorts, and feature vectors were extracted from bottleneck layers. Five OOD methods, including 1dimension (1D)-Subspace Analysis (1D-SSA), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Ridge Regression, Mahalanobis Distance (MD), and Sum of Squared Distances (SSD), were explored with 200 and 500-dimensional embeddings. Spectral discrepancy was used to discriminate in-distribution (IND) from OOD samples. Performance was measured via cross-validation, holdout samples, and an independent clinical dataset. 1D-SSA was the most effective approach. In the sarcoma-IND/brain tumor-OOD setting, the framework achieved an AUROC of 0.975 and True Negative Rate (TNR)@95TPR of 0.930, and an AUROC of 0.9569 and TNR@95TPR of 0.8660 for the brain tumor-IND/sarcoma-OOD setting. On the independent clinical test set, the method yielded a mean AUROC of 0.976, a DE of 0.032, an FPR@95TPR of 0.065, and a TNR@95TPR of 0.935. These results show deep representation-based OOD detection as a practical quality-control layer for clinical-grade methylation-based tumor classification systems.
picks.why: An out-of-distribution detection framework for DNA methylation-based tumor classifiers addresses a critical quality-control gap in clinical cancer genomics pipelines using deep representation learning.

picks.title: Stationary Action Principles for Neuronal Growth
picks.abstract: Neuronal growth is guided by biochemical, mechanical, and geometrical cues while being influenced by stochastic fluctuations in cytoskeletal dynamics, adhesion, and growth cone sensing. Here, we develop two complementary variational descriptions of mechanically guided axonal growth. First, for neurons growing on periodic parallel micropatterns, we use Langevin and Fokker–Planck models to derive a stochastic path action incorporating deterministic substrate guidance and random fluctuations. The probability of a growth trajectory decreases exponentially with this action, and the most probable trajectories correspond to minimum action paths for fixed boundary conditions. Second, for axons growing on substrates with spatially varying stiffness, we show that stiffness dependent traction generates mechanical guidance and axonal turning at stiffness interfaces. In the quasi-static limit, this response leads to a Fermat-like spatial action with an effective axonal refractive index determined by the traction and substrate stiffness relationship. The resulting framework predicts axonal refraction across stiffness boundaries, including an approximate Snell-like relation and a critical angle condition. Although the stochastic and Fermat-like actions have distinct physical meanings and ranges of validity, both describe how substrate mechanics constrain axonal trajectories. These results connect measurable quantities, including drift, diffusion, stiffness, traction, and growth direction, to global properties of axonal paths and provide a framework for designing biomimetic substrates for controlled neuronal growth and regeneration.
picks.why: Variational/stochastic action principles for axonal growth guided by substrate mechanics connect biophysical modeling to measurable growth cone dynamics, a nice mechanistic systems biology angle outside sequencing.

picks.title: scPyviewer: a Python-native interactive viewer from AnnData single-cell data
picks.abstract: Motivation: Interactive web tools enabling non-programmers to explore single-cell datasets, embeddings, gene expression, metadata, and marker genes are standard laboratory infrastructure. However, actively maintained tools (e.g., ShinyCell, ScRDAVis, sCIRCLE) rely on R Shiny and require Seurat objects. Python/scanpy, the dominant framework for single-cell RNA-seq and spatial analysis, lacks a lightweight, native option pairing a shareable viewer with a scriptable Python API. Sharing scanpy results currently requires converting to Seurat or sharing code notebooks. Results: We present scPyviewer, a web viewer that ingests AnnData objects directly and reproduces incumbent interaction patterns within the Python stack. In a feature-parity audit against three R Shiny tools, scPyviewer matches or exceeds baseline capabilities (7/7), uniquely offering native AnnData ingestion without conversion and cross-dataset comparison over shared genes and matched cell types. Benchmark tests across three datasets (22,315 to ~313,000 cells) show scPyviewer renders every core view faster (up to 3.6x speedup) using lower memory (5.2x lower on the smallest dataset). On 313,000 cells, scPyviewer completes all views while Seurat exhausts an 8 GB memory limit and fails. Beyond the app, scPyviewer exposes a Python API returning Matplotlib figures and pandas tables for publication-ready output. Availability and implementation: Implemented in Python 3.11 (scanpy 1.11.5, anndata 0.12.19, streamlit 1.59.2, plotly 6.9.0) with a one-command interface to reproduce benchmarks, figures, and launch the app. Source code: https://github.com/xuan13hao/scPyviewer.git
picks.why: A lightweight Python-native interactive viewer for AnnData objects fills a real gap for scanpy users who currently must convert to Seurat to share single-cell results.

picks.title: pyTransRate: 1 reference-free quality assessment of de novo transcriptome assemblies with current aligners and quantifiers
picks.abstract: Summary: The original software TransRate scores a de novo transcriptome assembly by mapping the reads it was built from back to it, with no reference required. Its last release (1.0.3) depends on Ruby 2.2 and on aligner and quantifier versions that can no longer be installed on most systems. pyTransRate is a Python reimplementation of the TransRate method built on snap-aligner 2.0.5 and salmon 2.7.0. In 5,031 paired comparisons (39 assembly-level metrics on each of 129 public assemblies), it reproduces the original sequence metrics and read counts exactly and ranks assemblies consistently with 1.0.3 (Spearman rho = 0.94 for assembly score, 0.98 for good-mapping rate), although its read-based scores are not numerically interchangeable with the original. It also reads gzip- and bgzip-compressed input directly. Availability and Implementation: pyTransRate is implemented in Python 3 and is freely available under the MIT license at https://github.com/macmanes-lab/pytransrate. It runs on Linux and macOS; snap-aligner and salmon are installed from Bioconda. Supplementary information: Supplementary data are available online. Supplementary Table S1 lists the assembly and read accessions for every assembly analyzed; Supplementary Table S2 gives per-assembly values from both implementations.
picks.why: A modernized, dependency-free reimplementation of TransRate gives de novo transcriptome assemblers a reference-free QC tool that actually still runs on current systems.

picks.title: ACOR: incremental evidence accumulation towards real-time DNA storage reconstruction
picks.abstract: DNA offers high-density, durable storage by encoding digital information into synthetic strands and retrieving it through sequencing. Sequence reconstruction combines noisy copies of each strand before downstream decoding. Conventional offline methods typically reconstruct completed read clusters, separating reconstruction from ongoing read collection. Streaming reconstruction offers a way to overlap evidence processing with sequencing and reduce the computation remaining before downstream decoding. We present ACOR, a streaming consensus reconstruction method that records k-mer transitions and boundary support in a persistent ledger, then decodes through length-constrained beam search and priority-based selection at cluster closure. Evaluation on real and simulated DNA-storage datasets showed competitive recovery. On our own short-read next-generation sequencing (NGS) wet-lab library, ACOR combined near-complete recovery with second-scale reconstruction of more than ten million reads. A smaller public benchmark was completed in a fraction of a second. Parallel ACOR achieved speedups of tens to over a thousand-fold relative to the tested serial baseline configurations. Sparse storage reduced high-context memory requirements, while parallel execution accelerated reconstruction computation. ACOR is designed for streaming readout pipelines that process assigned reads while sequencing continues.
picks.why: A streaming consensus-reconstruction algorithm for DNA storage achieves near real-time decoding of noisy synthetic DNA reads, relevant to the computational side of DNA-based data storage.

picks.title: The uneven rise of AI-generated web content
picks.abstract: In less than five years, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has dramatically reshaped the public-facing web. Using a sample of more than 5 million crawlable webpages, we demonstrate that the share containing AI-generated text has increased precipitously, but unevenly. Our analyses reveal substantial differences in AI composition across language and domain categories (e.g., .edu, .com, or .gov). A higher fraction of English-language webpages contain AI-generated text compared to pages in other languages, and prevalence is substantially lower on .gov and .edu domains compared to .com. These distinctions persist even after accounting for compositional effects. We also find heterogeneity based on a page's position in the connectivity structure of the web. AI-generated text is most common and has increased most rapidly in pages that are the least central in the graph, which drives much of the overall growth in AI-generated text. A slower increase has taken place for more central pages, with the most central tier emerging as the least likely to contain AI-generated text. Methodologically, we use multiple AI detection tools, and generate estimates using a Bayesian hierarchical model that incorporates corrections for the detectors' statistical properties (both false positives and false negatives) and allows for different detector performance across groups, while propagating uncertainty in detector error rates into prevalence estimates. Our work suggests that AI is a prominent, but varied, contributor to public information and internet-based communication.
picks.why: A large-scale Bayesian measurement-error-corrected analysis finds AI-generated text is growing fastest on the least-central, least-trafficked parts of the web, a surprising structural finding about the internet's information ecosystem.

picks.title: Balanced State Subspaces for Mamba-2 State Compression
picks.abstract: Mamba-2 compresses all context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors quantize state values or prune state coordinates, scoring each channel independently in the native basis. We examine trained Mamba-2 states and find that energy is almost rank-one, but the output does not read the energetic directions: energy concentrates in a bias-like direction accumulated by the recurrence, while the content the output reads lives in a low-dimensional subspace that is not aligned with the state's coordinates. Even output-aware scores are computed coordinate by coordinate, so they miss the directions that determine the input–output map. Compression should therefore target the write–read subspace rather than individual coordinates. We propose \method, a post-training transform that instantiates balanced truncation with full controllability and observability Gramians and applies the rotation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition. Because the useful rank varies widely across layers, we further introduce HARP, which allocates ranks per layer from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers, improving both perplexity and retrieval over uniform budgets. Calibration takes a single forward pass, an order of magnitude faster than GHOST's released protocol, with lower peak memory. With HARP, \method halves the state dimension at an average WikiText-2 perplexity increase of 0.3 points (1.8\%) across 130M–2.7B, versus 1.6 (9.3\%) for GHOST, and the gap widens at 25\% retention.
picks.why: A balanced-truncation approach to compressing Mamba-2's recurrent state by finding the true write-read subspace nearly halves memory with much smaller perplexity loss than existing quantization/pruning methods.

picks.title: Close Races and Similarity Bias: A Bayesian Analysis of the Ranked Ballots for the Ballon d'Or
picks.abstract: The Ballon d'Or ranks players whose contributions have no common unit, so its results are often disputed. Regressions of award points describe associations but not how complete ballots arise or how likely a different winner would be. We propose a Bayesian mixture-of-experts model for partial rankings that learns nonlinear performance relationships, the number of voting styles and journalists' style memberships. A shared soft regression tree with style-specific leaf values lets styles evaluate the same season records differently on a common basis. Region-dependent mixing probabilities and journalist–nominee similarity terms separate geographic differences in voting styles from affinity within a style, and journalist- and rank-specific precisions capture remaining variation. We establish identification and consistency for the number of occupied styles under explicit conditions; simulations examine recovery, calibration and robustness to misspecification. Applied to all 176 published ballots from 2019 and 99 from 2024, the model compares award outcomes under changes in affinity and jury composition. For 2019, Messi's probability of winning with a new jury from the same countries rises from 0.49 to 0.76 when similarity terms are removed. For 2024, the direction of this change depends on whether affinities differ by region. Regional representation changes winner probabilities more than jury size.
picks.why: A Bayesian mixture-of-experts model for partial rankings quantifies how voter 'style' and regional affinity bias Ballon d'Or outcomes, a clever application of rank data modeling to a contested real-world judgment problem.

picks.title: Relaxed MEMs: Enhancing Borrowing in Multisource Exchangeability Models for Small Sample Applications
picks.abstract: Information sharing in clinical trials provides a promising way to increase trial efficiency, specifically in rare disease settings where sample sizes are small. Multisource Exchangeability Modeling (MEM) is a method that incorporates historical data from potentially multiple data sources, such as past trials, by exploring all possible configurations of exchangeability and provides a weight estimate for each configuration, allowing the user to quantify how much is being borrowed from each source. While MEMs have previously been shown to be asymptotically consistent, small sample sizes introduce uncertainty that naturally limits the amount of borrowing MEMs can facilitate. The proposed ``relaxed MEMs'' provide a mathematical framework for relaxing or removing those limits and allowing greater borrowing even in small-sample settings. Several relaxed MEM versions are proposed, and all strategies provide enhanced borrowing with minimal sacrifice in the bias and variance of the mean estimates. Specifically, the maximum absolute mean bias was 3.5\% (0.035) of the true mean in the two source continuous outcome settings and 6.4\% (0.032) of the true proportion in the two source binary outcome settings (absolute mean bias was 1.4\% (0.014) and 3.6\% (0.018), respectively, for traditional MEMs) and variance decreased relative to traditional MEMs across all exchangeable and small difference scenarios. The methods were then demonstrated using two endpoints from a series of phase II trials in cystic fibrosis.
picks.why: Relaxed Multisource Exchangeability Models loosen overly conservative borrowing limits in small-sample rare-disease trials, improving efficiency with minimal bias cost.

picks.title: Is Your LLM Relay Serving What It Claims? A low-cost and high-power test for LLM Relay Auditing
picks.abstract: Relay and reseller APIs have become a common way to access large language models (LLMs), yet users cannot directly verify whether they receive the models they request and pay for. This opacity motivates LLM relay auditing, but existing methods struggle to combine low cost, robustness to benign deployment changes, and statistically interpretable decisions under black-box access. To address these limitations, we propose distributional fingerprint auditing (DFA), a statistical method that requires only textual responses from suspect and trusted reference endpoints. DFA repeatedly queries semantically simple finite-choice probes and uses the resulting categorical response distributions to construct endpoint fingerprints. It compares the suspect and reference fingerprints probe by probe and aggregates the resulting evidence using the Cauchy combination test, yielding an approximate endpoint-level p-value for audit decisions at a prespecified nominal significance level. Using registered fingerprints of candidate models, a likelihood-based formulation further supports model attribution under full substitution and joint estimation of substitute identity and substitution ratio under constant-ratio mixed routing. Our benchmark includes 16 proprietary and open-weight LLMs from 10 model families. Across 240 ordered full-substitution pairs, DFA achieves high detection rates at a nominal significance level of \alpha=0.05, using five probes and 250 relay requests per audit with stored reference fingerprints. Configuration overrides can lead to rejection even when the served model remains unchanged, with effects varying across models and configurations. Simulations based on stored empirical fingerprints demonstrate accurate model attribution and estimate substitution ratios, with estimation error decreasing as the audit budget increases.
picks.why: A distributional-fingerprint statistical test lets users detect whether an LLM relay API is silently serving a substituted model, with calibrated p-values and substitution-ratio estimation.

picks.title: Causal DAG-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Physical Activity Maintenance: Using Prior Data to Inform Future Deployment
picks.abstract: Digital health interventions can provide scalable, personalized support for physical activity (PA), yet sustaining PA over the long-term remains difficult. Because affective experiences with PA are important for activity sustainment, we developed an online reinforcement learning (RL) system for the forthcoming ADAPT factorial trial that personalizes twice-daily activity suggestions aimed at improving affective associations with PA. This setting poses several challenges: participant-specific data are scarce relative to the candidate state space, important states and rewards are partially observed, interventions are frequent while the primary outcome is measured weekly, and activity suggestions can both improve PA-related experiences and increase intervention burden. We address these challenges using an expert-specified causal directed acyclic graph as an integrated RL design tool, guiding state construction, estimation of partially observed states, delayed credit assignment, and representation of beneficial and adverse intervention pathways. We further construct a longitudinal simulator calibrated from a prior micro-randomized trial to compare candidate RL designs under realistic state evolution, missingness, and participant heterogeneity before deployment. Together, this work illustrates how causal domain knowledge and prior trial data can make long-horizon, participant-specific RL more practical for digital health interventions targeting sustained behavior change.
picks.why: This causal-DAG-guided reinforcement learning design for a digital health physical-activity trial shows how domain knowledge and simulators can make long-horizon personalized interventions deployable despite sparse, delayed rewards.

picks.title: Dynamic Properties of Numerical Solution for Stochastic Epidemic Models with a Fully Implicit Form
picks.abstract: This paper establishes a fully implicit model to investigate the spread of epidemics and studies its dynamic properties, extending the semi-implicit model in Yang et al.(Commun. Nonlinear Sci. Numer. Simul., 152 (2026) 109140 ). We first employ the split-step backward Euler method to address the non-adaptability arising from backward Euler discretization and ensure the global convergence of the numerical solution. By linearizing the model, the computational cost is reduced at the expense of a slight increase in error, effectively avoiding complex iterative solution processes. Then, we derive the existence, uniqueness, positivity, and boundedness of the numerical solution, and obtain its global convergence order. On this basis, the extinction and persistence of the disease are investigated under three different scenarios. The results indicate that environmental noise is a key factor leading to disease extinction. Finally, numerical simulations visually verify the obtained theoretical conclusions.
picks.why: A fully implicit numerical scheme for stochastic epidemic models proves convergence and shows environmental noise can drive disease extinction.

picks.title: Bayesian Ordinal Analysis of Cereal Growth Stage Data from Oat Trials in Western Australia
picks.abstract: Growth stage in cereal field trials is usually scored on the Zadoks decimal scale. The score is ordinal, yet it is often analysed as if it were continuous, which can lead to misleading conclusions. Ordinal analysis of growth stage data has received little attention from biometricians or agronomists, and it is not straightforward when several plants are scored in each plot of a split-plot design. We analysed Zadoks scores recorded four weeks after sowing on ten plants per plot in two deep-sowing oat trials in Western Australia, using a Bayesian hierarchical ordinal model that carries the full split-plot structure and an AR1 x AR1 spatial covariance. The implementation was validated on simulated data, and the candidate models were compared by five-fold cross-validation over plots. Adding a random effect at the experimental-unit (plot) level changed the uncertainty of the sub-plot contrasts substantially, while the main-plot contrasts changed little. How that plot-level heterogeneity was modelled mattered much less. At either site, cross-validation could not separate the candidate models that carried a plot-level term, whether or not they included an AR1 x AR1 field or the blocking terms, and the autoregressive parameters were only weakly identified on this layout. Deeper sowing (80 and 120 mm against 30 mm) went with more advanced development at four weeks in both trials. Sowing at 120 mm rather than 30 mm raised the predicted probability of tillering from 0.04 to 0.24 at Wickepin and from 0.04 to 0.10 at Merredin. The depth effects were stable whether or not the spatial field was fitted, and under both the cumulative and the sequential ordinal family.
picks.why: A Bayesian hierarchical ordinal model with spatial structure analyzes cereal growth-stage scores from oat trials, showing deeper sowing accelerates early development.

picks.title: Finite-population inference for cross-fitted estimators of treatment contrasts in stratified multistage surveys
picks.abstract: Health surveys often sample clusters within strata and then individuals within clusters, and flexible outcome and treatment models complicate inference for adjusted contrasts from such surveys. We establish finite-population limit theory for survey-weighted augmented inverse-probability-weighted estimation within the double machine learning framework, using cross-fitting that keeps whole clusters together; a cross-fitted targeted maximum likelihood estimator inherits the results under additional targeting conditions. With first-stage clusters drawn by simple random sampling without replacement within strata, the theory allows arbitrary within-cluster dependence, appreciable sampling fractions, and many small strata, a few large strata, or both. Under bounded cluster sizes, a cluster-generation model and nuisance convergence-rate conditions, the estimator is asymptotically normal about the finite-population contrast, and a stability property derived from the cluster model controls the cross-fitting error without entropy conditions. The stratified ultimate-cluster variance estimator, without a first-stage finite-population correction, consistently estimates a with-replacement variance that is at least the without-replacement design variance of the normal limit, so the resulting intervals are asymptotically conservative, and exact when the excess is negligible. In simulations, near-nominal or higher coverage coexisted, in different settings, with remainder diagnostics above the study's negligibility benchmark and with inaccurate standard errors. In three Service Provision Assessment surveys from Malawi and Haiti, each frame treated as a fixed population and resampled 500 times, mean reported standard errors were 4%-20% larger than the empirical standard deviations, while coverage of whole-frame reference values was near or above nominal.
picks.why: New finite-population theory for cluster-respecting cross-fitted double machine learning estimators gives more honest variance estimates for treatment effects in stratified health surveys.

picks.title: Causal sensitivity analyses for indirect and spillover mediation effects in cluster-randomized trials: Application to a pragmatic trial on chronic pain management
picks.abstract: Causal mediation in cluster-randomized trials can clarify whether a cluster-level intervention changes patient outcomes through patient- and peer-level processes, but identification relies on untestable cross-world assumptions. We develop a two-part sensitivity analysis for violations of two distinct cross-world independence assumptions. The first component adapts bridge score sensitivity analysis to assess residual mediator-outcome confounding with clustered mediator exposures; the second uses a Gaussian copula to assess cross-world dependence between an individual's treated mediator and summaries of control-arm peer mediators. The resulting framework parameterizes unidentifiable dependence structures using interpretable correlation parameters and combines them with a flexible Bayesian nonparametric model to characterize the plausible range of the target estimands. A nested common-atoms enriched Dirichlet process models the observed data and supports posterior-predictive standardization. We apply the framework to the Pain Program for Active Coping and Training trial, a primary care-embedded cognitive behavioral therapy intervention for adults with chronic pain receiving long-term opioid therapy. The intervention had a negative total effect on twelve-month pain-related disability. The natural indirect and direct effect decomposition was sensitive to plausible directional residual confounding, whereas the spillover and individual mediation effect decomposition changed little across the copula sensitivity analyses and attributed most of the negative indirect signal to the individual's mediator. Jointly relaxing both assumptions substantially increased uncertainty about the pathways. The analysis supports an overall improvement in disability and a plausible individual pain-impact pathway, while showing that detailed mechanistic claims remain assumption-dependent.
picks.why: A two-part sensitivity analysis for cross-world mediation assumptions in a cluster-randomized chronic pain trial shows mechanistic pathway claims are highly assumption-dependent.

picks.title: Penalized Cause-Specific Hazard Regression under Competing Risks: An Elastic Net Approach Using SANAD Trial Data
picks.abstract: Competing risks analysis is an important framework for studying time-to-event data in the presence of multiple, mutually exclusive events. Traditional methods, such as non-parametric estimators and proportional hazards models, may not adequately capture complex hazard patterns or provide stable estimates in practical settings. In this study, we propose a parametric approach based on the generalized exponential regression model for competing risks data. The model allows flexible hazard shapes and incorporates covariate effects through a regression structure. To improve estimation stability, we integrate elastic net regularization into the likelihood framework. The proposed method is evaluated through simulation studies and applied to a real dataset. The results indicate that the elastic net approach provides more stable and precise estimates compared to standard maximum likelihood estimation. Overall, the proposed framework offers a flexible and practical approach for analyzing competing risks data.
picks.why: An elastic-net-regularized generalized exponential regression for competing risks improves estimate stability over standard cause-specific hazard models in a stroke trial dataset.

picks.title: Estimating the Effect of a Low Nicotine Standard on Smoking Behavior in the U.S. Population
authors: Milena I. Silva (Division of Biostatistics and Health Data Science
Lianne K. Siegel (Division of Biostatistics and Health Data Science
Katherine J. Li (Division of Biostatistics and Health Data Science
David M. Vock (Division of Biostatistics and Health Data Science
Eric C. Donny (Wake Forest University School of Medicine)
Jennifer W. Tidey (Center for Alcohol and Addiction Studies
Joseph S. Koopmeiners (Division of Biostatistics and Health Data Science
Jared D. Huling (Division of Biostatistics and Health Data Science
picks.abstract: In January of 2025, the FDA announced a proposed rule to set a nationwide nicotine standard of 0.7 mg/cigarette that would reduce nicotine levels in cigarettes by 95\%. Past trials comparing very-low nicotine content (VLNC) cigarettes and normal nicotine content (NNC) cigarettes consistently found randomization to receive VLNC cigarettes reduces cigarette consumption. However, these results are not intrinsically generalizable, as the trials exhibited partial treatment non-adherence and were not designed as representative samples of the United States (U.S.) population of people who smoke (PWS). Existing transportability methods do not account for non-adherence or target a different estimand. Additionally, non-adherence cannot be directly observed and must be estimated using biomarkers of nicotine exposure, and different biomarkers were collected across trials. To estimate the effect of full adherence to a low nicotine standard in the U.S. population of PWS, we develop a novel inverse odds weighting estimator for transporting an intervention's effect to a fully adherent target population, and propose a bivariate mixture model approach for estimating adherence using biomarkers that allows partial missingness in one of the biomarkers. Finally, we use our method to transport inferences from seven trials investigating VLNC cigarettes to a representative sample of U.S. PWS.
picks.why: A novel transportability estimator accounting for treatment non-adherence estimates how a near-total nicotine reduction standard would affect smoking behavior in the broader U.S. population.

picks.title: Bayesian Recovery Trajectories Following Forced Sexual Experience: Healthcare Access and Social Support Among Women
picks.abstract: \textbfBackground. Women who experience forced sexual violence face elevated risks of poor mental and physical health, but whether long-term health follows distinct trajectories and whether healthcare access and social support differentiate them remains unclear. \textbfMethods. We analyzed 1,848 women from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), followed from adolescence into adulthood. An identified Bayesian mixture model classified joint mental and physical health burden trajectories from six repeated indicators. Bayesian logistic models estimated associations of forced sexual experience, healthcare access, social support, and demographics with trajectory membership. Robustness was assessed across three mixture specifications and four- and five-class alternatives. \textbfResults. We retained three classes: low-burden/resilient (27.2\% posterior mean weight), moderate/worsening burden (43.2\%), and high chronic burden (29.7\%). All specifications converged (\hatR=1.00) with well-separated classes; four- and five-class alternatives had convergence problems or an unstable additional class. Forced sexual experience was associated with higher posterior odds of high chronic burden (OR = 3.78, 95\% credible interval [CrI] 2.84–5.04) and moderate/worsening burden (OR = 1.63, 95\% CrI 1.26–2.12). Better healthcare access and greater social connectedness were independently associated with lower posterior odds of high chronic burden. \noindent\textbfConclusions. Long-term health after forced sexual experience follows heterogeneous trajectories. Healthcare access and social connectedness distinguish more favorable trajectories and represent modifiable targets for trauma-informed, longitudinal, survivor-centered care.
picks.why: A Bayesian mixture model identifies three distinct long-term health trajectories after forced sexual violence, with healthcare access and social support as modifiable protective factors.

picks.title: Practical Guidelines for Goodness-of-Fit Testing for Right-Censored Data
picks.abstract: In survival studies, right censoring often prevents the observation of subjects' complete outcomes, complicating inference about the underlying distribution. Evaluating whether a given distribution adequately fits right-censored data is therefore essential. However, guidance on the relative performance of available goodness-of-fit tests under different data conditions remains limited. In this work, we present a comparative assessment of three classical goodness-of-fit tests adapted for right-censored data: Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling, and Cramér-von Mises. Through an extensive simulation study, we investigate how factors such as the proportion of right-censored observations, sample size, and distributional symmetry influence the statistical power of each test. All procedures were implemented using the R package GofCens, and power estimates were obtained from extensive replicated simulations. The results identify the settings in which each test exhibits superior performance, providing practical, evidence-based recommendations for test selection in survival analysis. These recommendations are summarized as user-oriented guidelines and complemented by a concise graphical cheat sheet, enabling practitioners to quickly identify the most suitable test for their specific application.
picks.why: A simulation study gives practical guidance on when Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling, or Cramér-von Mises goodness-of-fit tests perform best for right-censored survival data.

picks.title: Personal preference or system role? Battery swapping among UK electric vehicle users
picks.abstract: Battery swapping replaces a depleted EV battery with a charged one, reducing waiting time and enabling off-peak charging. Evidence on acceptance, however, remains concentrated in Asian markets, and most studies examine individual adoption intentions. This study asks whether current UK EV users judge swapping differently as a purchase option and as a technology for the transport system. Using Behavioural Reasoning Theory, an integrated choice and latent variable model, and latent class analysis, we analyse perceived usefulness, energy-system concerns, practical barriers, and satisfaction with current charging. Usefulness and energy-system concerns relate more strongly to expectations about the system. Battery compatibility and station coverage relate more strongly to personal preference, while spare battery costs relate to expectations about network viability. User groups differ in how they balance benefits, barriers, and satisfaction with existing charging. Policy should address driver barriers and network viability as distinct but connected priorities.
picks.why: A choice-latent-variable model finds UK EV users evaluate battery swapping differently as a personal purchase decision versus a system-level transport technology.

picks.title: Reconstructing the Human Development Index at the Individual Level from Survey Microdata: Development and Validation of a Methodology
authors: Natalia Veronez da Cunha (Universidade do Planalto Catarinense
picks.abstract: This study proposes and validates a methodology for reconstructing the Human Development Index (HDI) from individual-level survey microdata, enabling disaggregated estimates for demographic subpopulations while maintaining coherence with the official HDI. Data from 40,185 respondents in 21 countries from the European Social Survey (ESS7, 2014) were analysed, combined with World Bank indicators for life expectancy, gross national income per capita, and expected years of schooling. The health dimension was estimated from national life expectancy, adjusted by self-rated health; income, by a lognormal multiplier calibrated by the Gini coefficient; and education, by combining observed and expected years of schooling. The dimensions were aggregated by geometric mean, weighted by sampling weights, with confidence intervals estimated via the delta method. Among the 39,706 individuals with valid data (98.8%), the reconstructed HDI showed high agreement with the official 2014 HDI, with a mean absolute error of 0.0099 and a Pearson correlation of 0.917. Consistent differences across subgroups evidenced the methodology's convergent validity and its capacity to produce disaggregated estimates of human development, expanding the HDI's potential for analyses of socioeconomic and demographic inequalities.
picks.why: A method to reconstruct individual-level HDI scores from survey microdata achieves high agreement with official national HDI values, enabling disaggregated development analysis.
